note.explanation: In an exothermic reaction, more energy is released when bonds form than is taken in when bonds break. In an endothermic reaction, more energy is taken in breaking bonds than is released forming bonds.
examples: For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 571.6 kJ, heat is released and ΔH is negative.
Melting ice takes in heat, so it is endothermic.
note.checkAnswer: Breaking a bond absorbs energy, so it is endothermic.
note.simple: Breaking bonds takes in energy; forming bonds gives out energy. Compare the two amounts to decide whether the whole reaction takes in or gives out energy.
note.checkQuestion: Is bond breaking endothermic or exothermic?
note.title: Energy changes in reactions
steps: Identify the energy needed to break the reactant bonds.
Identify the energy released when product bonds form.
Subtract: ΔH = energy absorbed − energy released.
A negative ΔH means heat is released; a positive ΔH means heat is absorbed.
note.answer: Exothermic reactions release heat and have a negative ΔH. Endothermic reactions absorb heat and have a positive ΔH.

options: The reaction absorbs more energy breaking bonds than it releases forming bonds.
The reaction releases more energy forming bonds than it absorbs breaking bonds.
The reaction has no bond breaking.
The reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings.
mcqs.stem: Which statement best explains why a reaction is exothermic?
rationales: This describes an endothermic overall energy change, not an exothermic one.
This is correct: the energy released is greater than the energy absorbed.
Chemical reactions generally involve bond breaking as well as bond formation.
Absorbing heat from the surroundings describes an endothermic reaction.

mcqs.stem: What is the sign of ΔH for an exothermic reaction?
rationales: A positive ΔH indicates that heat is absorbed overall.
A negative ΔH indicates that heat is released overall.
ΔH is zero only when there is no net enthalpy change.
The sign can be stated from whether heat is absorbed or released.

mcqs.stem: A reaction releases heat to its surroundings. What is most likely to happen to the surroundings?
rationales: This is correct: released heat warms the surroundings.
The surroundings tend to cool when a reaction absorbs heat.
Heat is transferred in this situation, so this is incorrect.
The state of the products does not determine whether the surroundings warm.

options: Bond breaking has no energy change.
Bond breaking always forms a new bond.
mcqs.stem: What happens to energy when a chemical bond is broken?
rationales: This is correct: energy must be supplied to separate bonded atoms.
Bond breaking requires energy rather than releasing it.
Breaking a bond requires energy, so the change is not zero.
Bond breaking separates atoms; bond formation is a different process.

mcqs.stem: For a reaction, 587 kJ is absorbed breaking bonds and 598 kJ is released forming bonds. What is ΔH?
rationales: This has the wrong sign for a reaction releasing more energy than it absorbs.
This is correct: ΔH = 587 − 598 = −11 kJ.
This gives only the energy released in bond formation, not the net change.
This does not subtract the released energy from the absorbed energy correctly.

options: The reverse reaction releases the same amount of heat.
The reverse reaction absorbs the same amount of heat.
The reverse reaction has no energy change.
The reverse reaction must have a different ΔH sign and magnitude.
mcqs.stem: An exothermic reaction has ΔH = −120 kJ. What is the enthalpy change for the reverse reaction?
rationales: The reverse reaction has the opposite direction of energy transfer, so it absorbs heat.
This is correct: reversing the reaction changes the sign, giving +120 kJ.
Reversing the reaction does not make its energy change zero.
The magnitude remains 120 kJ, while the sign changes.

options: A reaction forming stronger bonds than the bonds broken is likely exothermic.
A reaction forming weaker bonds than the bonds broken is always exothermic.
mcqs.stem: Which statement agrees with the bond-energy explanation of an exothermic reaction?
rationales: This is correct: stronger product bonds release more energy when formed.
If less energy is released forming weaker bonds, the reaction is not necessarily exothermic.
Bond formation releases energy; it does not absorb it.
Bond breaking absorbs energy rather than releasing it.

mcqs.stem: The reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) releases 571.6 kJ. What is ΔH for forming one mole of liquid water?
rationales: This is correct: half the reaction forms one mole of water and ΔH is negative.
The sign is wrong because heat is released.
This is the heat change for forming two moles, not one.
This gives the wrong sign and is for two moles.

written.text:
Calculate the enthalpy change of the following chemical reaction.

H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2 HI(g)

Bond energies of H₂, I₂ and HI are 436,151, and -299 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively.

rubric.why: The energy absorbed to break the reactant bonds must be found first.
rubric.description: Calculate the energy absorbed in bond breaking.
rubric.how: Add 436 and 151 to obtain 587 kJ mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: Two HI bonds form, so their energy contribution must be counted twice.
rubric.description: Calculate the energy released in bond formation.

rubric.why: The net enthalpy change depends on comparing absorbed and released energy.
rubric.description: Subtract the energy released from the energy absorbed.
rubric.how: Calculate ΔH = 587 − 598.

rubric.why: The final value and its negative sign identify the reaction as exothermic.
rubric.description: Give the final enthalpy change with units.
rubric.how: State ΔH = −11 kJ mol⁻¹.

modelAnswer: Energy absorbed in breaking bonds = 436 + 151 = 587 kJ mol⁻¹
Energy released in forming bonds = 2 × (−299) = −598 kJ mol⁻¹
ΔH = energy absorbed + energy released = 587 + (−598)
ΔH = −11 kJ mol⁻¹

written.text: Why the chemical reaction between sodium metal and water proceeds violently?
written.finalAnswer: It is a highly exothermic reaction; the heat evolved can ignite the hydrogen produced.

rubric.why: Identifying the reaction as exothermic explains the release of heat.
rubric.description: State the energy nature of the reaction.
rubric.how: Say that it is highly exothermic or releases a large amount of heat.

rubric.why: The evolved heat and hydrogen explain why the reaction can proceed violently.
rubric.description: Relate the heat to the violent reaction.
rubric.how: Explain that the heat may ignite the hydrogen produced.

modelAnswer: The reaction between sodium and water is highly exothermic and evolves a large amount of heat.
The heat can ignite the hydrogen produced, so the reaction proceeds violently.

written.text: Is melting of ice an exothermic or endothermic change?

rubric.why: The classification is the required answer and follows from heat being absorbed.
rubric.description: Identify the type of change.
rubric.how: State that melting ice is endothermic.

modelAnswer: Melting of ice absorbs heat from its surroundings.
Therefore, melting of ice is an endothermic change.

written.finalAnswer: Yes; the reverse reaction absorbs the same amount of heat that the forward reaction releases.

rubric.why: The question asks whether reversal is possible.
rubric.description: Answer yes or no.
rubric.how: State that an exothermic reaction can be reversed.

rubric.why: The reverse direction has the opposite energy change.
rubric.description: Describe the energy change in reverse.
rubric.how: State that the reverse reaction absorbs the same amount of heat.

modelAnswer: Yes, an exothermic reaction can be reversed.
In the reverse direction, the same amount of heat is absorbed.

written.text: Calculate the enthalpy change for the formation of one mole of liquid water.

rubric.why: The balanced equation gives the amount of water corresponding to the stated heat change.
rubric.description: Use the reaction for forming liquid water.
rubric.how: Write 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 571.6 kJ.

rubric.why: The stated heat is for the formation of two moles of water.
rubric.description: Divide the heat change by two moles.
rubric.how: Calculate 571.6 ÷ 2.

rubric.why: Released heat gives a negative enthalpy change.
rubric.description: Use the correct sign.
rubric.how: Make the enthalpy change negative because the reaction is exothermic.

rubric.why: The final answer must be for one mole of liquid water.
rubric.description: State the enthalpy change per mole.
rubric.how: Give −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹.

modelAnswer: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 571.6 kJ
For 2 mol of H₂O, ΔH = −571.6 kJ
For 1 mol of H₂O, ΔH = −571.6 ÷ 2
ΔH = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹

written.text: Q6.2. Why is breaking of a bond an endothermic process?
written.finalAnswer: Energy must be absorbed to overcome the attractive forces holding the bonded atoms together.

rubric.why: Bond breaking requires an input of energy.
rubric.description: State what happens to energy.
rubric.how: Say that energy is absorbed or supplied.

rubric.why: This explains why energy is needed to break the bond.
rubric.description: Explain what the energy does.
rubric.how: Relate the energy to overcoming the attraction between bonded atoms or separating them.

modelAnswer: Energy must be absorbed to break a bond.
This energy overcomes the attractive forces holding the bonded atoms together, so bond breaking is endothermic.

written.text: Q8.2. Explain why the reaction between atmospheric gases oxygen and nitrogen does not take place under normal conditions? But in the presence of lightning these gases react to give NO. The reaction stops as soon as the lightning stops.
written.finalAnswer: The reaction is highly endothermic, so it needs the high energy supplied by lightning; when the lightning stops, this energy supply stops.

rubric.why: The endothermic nature accounts for the reaction needing a large energy input.
rubric.description: Identify the energy type of the reaction.
rubric.how: State that the reaction is highly endothermic.

rubric.why: Lightning supplies the energy needed for the reaction to occur.
rubric.description: Explain why the gases react during lightning.
rubric.how: Say that lightning provides enough energy for the reaction.

rubric.why: This explains why the reaction does not normally occur.
rubric.description: Relate the reaction to ordinary conditions.
rubric.how: State that normal conditions do not supply enough energy.

rubric.why: The energy supply explains why the reaction stops when lightning ends.
rubric.description: Explain why the reaction stops.
rubric.how: State that when lightning stops, the required energy supply is removed.

modelAnswer: The reaction between nitrogen and oxygen is highly endothermic.
Under normal conditions, there is not enough energy for the reaction to take place.
Lightning supplies enough energy for nitrogen and oxygen to react and form NO.
When the lightning stops, the energy supply stops, so the reaction stops.

written.text:
Q8.1. Find out the enthalpy change of the following reaction using the given data.

N₂ + O₂ → 2NO

Bond dissociation energy of N₂ = 958.38 kJ/mol
Bond dissociation energy of O₂ = 498 kJ/mol
Bond formation energy of NO = −626 kJ/mol

rubric.why: The energy absorbed to break the reactant bonds is needed for the calculation.
rubric.description: Add the reactant bond dissociation energies.
rubric.how: Calculate 958.38 + 498 = 1456.38 kJ mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: Two NO bonds form in the reaction, so the formation energy is counted twice.
rubric.description: Calculate the energy change for forming NO bonds.
rubric.how: Calculate 2 × (−626) = −1252 kJ mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: Combining absorbed and released energy gives the reaction's net change.
rubric.description: Combine the two energy contributions.

rubric.why: This is the numerical enthalpy change from the given data.
rubric.description: Give the calculated value.
rubric.how: Obtain +204.38.

rubric.why: The positive sign shows the reaction absorbs energy overall.
rubric.description: State the sign and units.
rubric.how: Give ΔH = +204.38 kJ mol⁻¹ and identify it as endothermic.

modelAnswer: Energy absorbed in breaking bonds = 958.38 + 498 = 1456.38 kJ mol⁻¹
Energy released in forming bonds = 2 × (−626) = −1252 kJ mol⁻¹
ΔH = energy absorbed + energy released
ΔH = +204.38 kJ mol⁻¹

written.text: Q8.3. Explain why formation of a bond is always an exothermic process.
written.finalAnswer: When a bond forms, the bonded atoms reach a lower-energy, more stable state and the excess energy is released.

rubric.why: The answer must refer to the formation of a bond.
rubric.description: Identify the process being explained.
rubric.how: State what happens when atoms form a bond.

rubric.why: Bonded atoms have lower energy and greater stability than separated atoms.
rubric.description: Describe the energy or stability of the bonded state.
rubric.how: Say that the atoms move to a lower-energy or more stable state.

rubric.why: This is the defining energy change of bond formation.
rubric.description: State what happens to energy.
rubric.how: Explain that energy is released or evolved.

rubric.why: Releasing energy makes the process exothermic.
rubric.description: Connect energy release to the term.
rubric.how: Conclude that bond formation is exothermic.

modelAnswer: When a bond forms, the atoms move into a lower-energy, more stable arrangement.
The excess energy is released to the surroundings.
A process that releases energy is exothermic.
Therefore, bond formation is exothermic.

examTips: Board questions may ask you to classify a change as exothermic or endothermic and state whether heat is absorbed or released.
For a bond-energy calculation, show energy absorbed in bond breaking, energy released in bond formation, and the net ΔH calculation.
Use a negative sign for heat released and a positive sign for heat absorbed; include the units and balance the equation.
For explanation questions, connect the energy change to bond breaking, bond formation, or heat transfer to the surroundings.

hints: Think about the direction of the reaction.
The reverse direction needs the same energy amount, but the energy transfer changes direction.

explain.title: Heat of a reaction
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “Heat, which is evolved or absorbed during a chemical reaction, is called the heat of that reaction.” A reaction may release heat or take it in.

explain.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
explain.body: Your textbook defines them this way: “Chemical reactions in which heat energy is evolved are called exothermic reactions while those in which heat energy is absorbed are called endothermic reactions.” Released heat warms the surroundings; absorbed heat can cool them.

explain.title: The sign of ΔH
explain.body: When heat is released, ΔH is negative. When heat is absorbed, ΔH is positive. For example, the section gives ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for carbon burning to form carbon dioxide.

explain.title: Bond energies explain the overall change
explain.body: Breaking bonds absorbs energy, while forming bonds releases energy. Compare the amounts: if bond formation releases more energy than bond breaking absorbs, the reaction is exothermic; if it releases less, the reaction is endothermic.

mistakes: Calling bond breaking exothermic: breaking a bond absorbs energy.
Using a positive ΔH for a reaction that releases heat, or a negative ΔH for one that absorbs heat.
Forgetting to count every bond in the balanced equation, such as the two HI bonds formed in the example.
Giving the energy for two moles when the question asks for one mole; divide by the number of moles and show the units.
Leaving out the sign or units in a bond-energy calculation.
